name: Olga Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew and check the tires and the route before the first load. I keep the old paper fault list clipped beside the radio; when a truck rattles on the lower turn, I know which mechanic to ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing the younger operators learn the mine before someone expects them to hurry. The shifts are long, but the pay is good and I have about eight months saved, so I do not have to change trades on someone else's timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a screen can sort a routine notice, but it must not decide whether a truck is safe to move. I will keep the machine's basic checks in my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift is mostly hands-on, and this mild picture does not say that work or pay changes much. I have eight months saved and plenty of nearby mines, so I do not see an immediate threat to my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my rotation and use the new screen only for the notices it sorts correctly. I would still compare each fault note with my paper list before I signed the handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job in this version. If nothing radical changes, I can keep working and leave the small time-saving tool to the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting the notices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it missed a tire fault or a radio closure, I would pause the truck and call the mechanic. I would write the missing detail on the fault list so the next shift saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the screen yourself or ask a younger operator to try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let one experienced driver test it on the lower turn first. If the notices matched the paper list for a month, I would use it for routine sorting and keep the safety check myself.

say: I would let a screen sort notices, but not make **safety decisions**.
I will keep basic machine checks **in my hands**.
think: I think my hands-on shift and pay **stay steady** here.
Eight months saved means I do not need to **rush trades**.
do: Keep my **current rotation** and check each notice against the paper fault list.
Let one driver test the screen on the **lower turn**.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own job and income in this mild case.
S0.quote: I will keep the machine's basic checks in my own hands.
fieldNote: Olga relies on a **paper fault list** and physical checks.
Her **eight-month savings** and nearby mines make the mild case manageable.
She allows a **one-shift test** after an experienced driver checks it.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and compare notices with the paper fault list
Wait one month before expanding screen use beyond routine notices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to show me the route on the ground before I changed a habit. I would also ask whether the company was changing lead hours when the planner moved to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI, and the hands-on part of my job looks safer than route planning for now. I worry that the paperwork attached to my lead role could shrink even while I am still driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask mechanic Tomas to demonstrate the planner on a normal route while my paper map was open. If another experienced driver agreed it was accurate, I would use it for one planning task, not replace my full handover routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the lead paperwork but do not expect my truck pay to disappear first. I would wait for a clear change in the rota before spending my savings on another course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which change would tell you that the planner had affected your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the lead allowance or paid handover time fell on my pay slip. If it did, I would ask the foreman whether the mine had cut the job or simply moved the notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner disagreed with your route, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop and check the road, the paper map and the radio call before following it. If the planner had missed a closure, I would report the error and keep the current route until the foreman checked it.

say: I would ask the foreman to show me the route **before I changed** a habit.
I would ask whether software changes **lead hours**.
think: I do not use AI, and my work is **mostly hands-on**.
I worry the lead paperwork could **shrink first**.
do: Ask mechanic Tomas to demonstrate the **planner** on a normal route.
Use one planning task only after another driver **confirms accuracy**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about paperwork, but truck pay looks steady for now.
S1.quote: I would ask the foreman to show me the route on the ground before I changed a habit.
fieldNote: Olga resists unfamiliar software until a mechanic demonstrates it **on site**.
She worries about **lead paperwork** more than immediate driving loss.
Her pay-slip checks focus on **allowance and handover time**.

steps.text: Wait for the foreman to demonstrate the planner on a normal route
Keep the paper map and full handover routine during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI comes first and robots follow around three years later. I would ask the mine to offer a paid mechanic apprenticeship before it starts changing truck shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my truck job could be at risk by 2031 because robots can do the hands-on task I am paid for. I have eight months saved and plenty of nearby mines, but I would rather start learning a trade before the pit changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask a mechanic to explain the paid diesel-maintenance apprenticeship and enroll if it teaches real repairs. In 2029, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical service work only if the mine named the wage and how long it expected to need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace my main source of pay within five years. Eight months saved and several mines nearby give me some control, but I do not want to wait until everyone else is applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship is mostly computer records or diagnostic work that AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask whether the job includes touching, inspecting and repairing equipment. AGI could take the records and diagnosis, and I cannot assume physical service jobs will stay after the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine has no paid apprenticeship by 2029, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my truck job and ask the other nearby mines about their mechanic intakes. I would not stop earning to take a course that had no employer or wage at the end.

say: I would explain that robots arrive about **three years** after thinking AI.
I would ask for a paid **mechanic apprenticeship** before shifts change.
think: I expect robots to threaten my **truck job by 2031**.
My savings and nearby mines give me **some control**.
do: Enroll in the paid **diesel-maintenance apprenticeship** if it teaches real repairs.
In 2029, apply for service work with a **named wage and duration**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could replace my main income task within five years.
S2.quote: I expect my truck job could be at risk by 2031 because robots can do the hands-on task I am paid for.
fieldNote: Olga sees robots as a **direct threat** to her main paid task.
Her savings and local alternatives give her choices, not a **guarantee**.
She distinguishes repairs from **records and diagnosis** that AGI can do.

steps.text: Enroll in the paid diesel-maintenance apprenticeship if it teaches repairs
Apply for physical service work with a named wage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives a worker time to train if the mine pays for a course. I would ask the foreman to say plainly what physical work the mine expects to need after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have eight years before the robot date, which gives me time to learn diesel repair while I still have a good wage. I do not want to move into records after AGI, and I would need to know whether repair jobs last beyond 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a paid mechanic apprenticeship before 2031 and keep my haul-truck qualification current. In 2032, the first year after AGI arrives, I would apply for repair shifts only if the work was physical and the wage and duration were written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because there is time to prepare, but no one can promise a repair job will last after robots arrive. I would keep my current wage while training rather than leave the truck for a temporary title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the apprenticeship rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mechanic to show me an ordinary service shift and tell me what a new worker earns. I would also ask whether nearby mines still need people after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if repair work looks temporary, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the wage covered my costs and gave me time to find another position before the robot date. If it did not, I would stay with my current crew and keep checking other mines.

say: I would say five years allows **paid training** before the change.
I would ask what physical work remains after **2034**.
think: I can learn repairs while keeping **my current wage**.
I will not treat records work as a fallback after **AGI**.
do: In 2032, apply only with clear **wage and duration** in writing.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because training time helps, but repair work may be temporary.
S3.quote: I would have eight years before the robot date, which gives me time to learn diesel repair while I still have a good wage.
fieldNote: Olga sees eight years as **time to learn** while earning.
She does not treat records roles as safe **after AGI**.
She wants **job duration and pay** before leaving her current role.

steps.text: Complete the paid diesel mechanic apprenticeship before 2031
Apply for physical repair shifts with written terms in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine has a decade to pay people to learn trades before the thinking tools arrive. I would also ask for the actual schedule for robots, because the hands-on work changes about three years after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 40 when robots are expected, and my savings and local job options give me time to plan. I would still want proof that a repair job has real physical work and a wage after 2039 before I changed mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and ask the mine whether its paid repair course leads to jobs at other sites. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would compare written duties and wages before deciding whether to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income is good and I have years to prepare. I would not leave a proven job until a new employer showed me a vacancy that paid enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before accepting a repair role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the employer to name the physical tasks, pay and likely duration of the position. I would ask whether the mine expects robots to take that work in 2039 or earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the employer cannot say how long the job will last, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay in my current role and ask nearby mines about their training routes. I would wait for a written offer with a wage before moving.

say: I would ask the mine to pay for **trade training** before AGI.
I would ask for the robot **schedule** too.
think: My pay and local options give me **time to plan**.
I want proof of repair wages after **2039**.
do: Ask whether the paid repair course leads to **other-site jobs**.
In 2037, compare written duties and **wages** before moving.
feel: I feel **calm** because my income is good and I have years to prepare.
S4.quote: I would not leave a proven job until a new employer showed me a vacancy that paid enough.
fieldNote: Olga treats the decade as **time to plan**, not automatic security.
She wants repair duties, **pay and duration** in writing.
Her strong savings let her wait for a vacancy instead of **rushing**.

steps.text: Keep working while checking paid course outcomes at other sites
Wait for a written repair offer with a stated wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach the truck work by about 2031. A paid apprenticeship, a clear wage and enough notice would help me move toward repair work without giving up my income too soon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want a mechanic to show me the work before I sign a course form. I can learn a trade, but I will not leave my crew for a title that has no pay or duration behind it.

headlineQuote: I want a mechanic to show me the work before I sign a course form.
portrait: Olga Weber is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
She earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of savings.
Many nearby mines give her **other options** if her work changes.
She **avoids AI tools** and prefers to learn from experienced mechanics.
She wants **paid apprenticeships** and clear wages before leaving the truck.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves about five years before robots could change Olga's paid truck work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, clear wage and enough notice would help Olga move toward repair work without losing income too soon.
